title: Special HF paths and ionospheric waves
blurb: Explain transequatorial, long-path, chordal-hop, sporadic-E and ground-wave propagation, and what ordinary and extraordinary waves are.

E3B01.why: TEP crosses the **geomagnetic equator** on a path perpendicular to it, usually 2,000 – 3,000 miles.
E3B01.trap: Paths along the equator or at antipodes are not TEP.

E3B02.why: TEP reaches about **5,000 miles** at most.

E3B03.why: TEP appears in the **afternoon or early evening**.

E3B04.why: The ionosphere creates ordinary and extraordinary waves: **independently propagating, elliptically polarized**.
E3B04.trap: They aren't long-path/short-path or rare/common skip.

E3B05.why: The D layer absorbs low bands by day, so a path **entirely in darkness** carries 160 m best.

E3B06.why: Long-path openings are most frequent on **40 m and 20 m**.

E3B07.why: A lower takeoff angle makes each hop **cover more distance**.
E3B07.trap: The critical frequency belongs to the layer, and a lower angle raises the path's MUF rather than lowering it.

E3B09.why: Sporadic E peaks **around the solstices, especially the summer solstice**.

E3B10.why: Chordal hop skips ground reflections, so it has **less loss than multi-hop**, which bounces off the Earth.

E3B11.why: Sporadic E occurs **between sunrise and sunset**.

E3B12.why: Chordal hop is **successive ionospheric refractions** with no ground reflection between them.
E3B12.trap: It's not off-bearing propagation or equator crossing.

E3B13.why: Ground waves need **vertical polarization**: horizontal fields are shorted out by the ground.
